title: Discrete Mathematics
description: Discrete Mathematics is one common foundation across Computer Science, Mathematics, and Computer Engineering. Students translate informal claims into precise logical, set-theoretic, relational, graph, and automata models, then prove, count, compute, and communicate those models. The course moves from mathematical language, logic, sets, functions, and proof through combinatorics, discrete probability, number theory, recurrences, graphs, Boolean algebra, automata, computability, and complexity. One rigorous core serves all three degrees. Computer Science emphasizes invariants, algorithm analysis, automata, and security, Mathematics emphasizes bijections, generating functions, and theorem-quality exposition, and Computer Engineering emphasizes Boolean minimization, state machines, coding, and network models.

topics.title: Course Orientation, Mathematical Language, and Discrete Structures
topics.description: This opening unit establishes the objects, notation, and habits that make discrete mathematics a precise language for computing, mathematics, and digital engineering.

children.title: What Discrete Mathematics Studies
children.description: Students distinguish finite and countable structures from continuous models and see why discrete abstraction is central to algorithms and hardware.

children.title: Examples from programs, networks, circuits, and proofs
Abstraction from a real system to a mathematical model
Definitions, Statements, and Notation
children.description: Precise definitions control what may be assumed and what must be proved. Notation makes those commitments compact and checkable.

children.title: Set, sequence, summation, and logical notation
Problem-Solving and Computational Exploration
children.description: Good discrete problem solving alternates examples, conjectures, proof, and computation without confusing experimental evidence with proof.

children.title: Python or SageMath checks with reproducible reasoning

topics.title: Propositional Logic and Logical Equivalence
topics.description: Propositional logic supplies a formal language for combining claims and deciding when an argument, specification, or circuit is valid.

children.title: Propositions and Connectives
children.description: Students translate ordinary statements into formulas whose truth depends on well-defined logical operations.

children.title: Negation, conjunction, disjunction, implication, and biconditional
Truth Tables and Equivalence
children.description: Truth tables expose the behavior of compound statements and support systematic simplification.

children.title: Inference, Satisfiability, and Applications
children.description: Rules of inference turn accepted premises into justified conclusions and connect logic to verification and SAT solving.

children.title: Validity, sound inference rules, and fallacies

topics.title: Predicate Logic, Quantifiers, and Formal Inference
topics.description: Predicate logic extends propositional reasoning to properties of objects, making it possible to express mathematical definitions and program specifications accurately.

children.title: Predicates, Domains, and Free Variables
children.description: A predicate becomes meaningful only relative to its variables and domain, so students learn to make both explicit.

children.title: Quantifiers and Negation
children.description: Universal and existential quantifiers express scope. Careful negation prevents common errors in proofs and specifications.

children.title: Formal Inference and Specification
children.description: Quantified inference supports theorem proving, database queries, contracts, and requirements.

topics.title: Sets, Functions, Relations, and Cardinality
topics.description: Sets, functions, relations, and cardinality describe collections and mappings, the structural vocabulary behind data types, databases, graphs, and modern mathematics.

children.title: Sets and Set Operations
children.description: Students use sets to represent collections and manipulate them with identities that parallel logic.

children.title: Membership, subsets, power sets, and products
Functions and Mappings
children.description: Functions formalize deterministic input-output behavior and support counting, equivalence, and algorithm design.

children.title: Relations and Cardinality
children.description: Relations organize objects by similarity or order, while cardinality compares the sizes of finite and infinite sets.

children.title: Partial orders, Hasse diagrams, and closures
Finite, countably infinite, and uncountable sets

topics.title: Proof Techniques and Mathematical Writing
topics.description: Proof is the course's central practice: it converts plausible patterns into conclusions that remain correct for every permitted case.

children.title: Direct Proof, Cases, and Existence
children.description: Students learn constructive proof patterns that follow definitions and expose why a statement is true.

children.title: Contrapositive, Contradiction, and Counterexample
children.description: Indirect methods simplify difficult implications, while one valid counterexample defeats a universal claim.

children.title: Mathematical Writing and Proof Review
children.description: A proof must be logically complete and readable by another person, not merely convincing to its author.

children.title: Definitions cited at the point of use
Clear variable scope and quantified claims
Proof critique, revision, and LaTeX conventions

topics.title: Mathematical Induction, Recursion, and Invariants
topics.description: Induction and invariants reason about recursively generated objects and processes that evolve through repeated steps.

children.title: Ordinary and Strong Induction
children.description: Induction proves an infinite family of statements by connecting each case to established earlier cases.

children.title: Recursive Definitions and Structural Induction
children.description: Recursive definitions build large objects from smaller ones. Structural induction mirrors that construction.

children.title: Recursively defined strings, trees, and formulas
Structural induction over syntax and data structures
Invariants and Algorithm Correctness
children.description: An invariant identifies what remains true as a loop, protocol, or state machine changes.

topics.title: Counting Principles and Advanced Combinatorics
topics.description: Combinatorics develops principled ways to count possibilities without listing them, a key skill in probability, complexity, coding, and design.

children.title: Basic Counting Principles
children.description: Students decompose a counting problem into disjoint alternatives or sequential choices.

children.title: Binomial coefficients and the binomial theorem
Bijections, Pigeonhole, and Inclusion-Exclusion
children.description: Structural counting arguments reveal why two sets have the same size and correct for overlap.

children.title: Generating Functions and Combinatorial Identities
children.description: Generating functions encode sequences algebraically and turn recurrence or selection problems into coefficient calculations.

topics.title: Discrete Probability, Random Variables, and Stochastic Reasoning
topics.description: Discrete probability quantifies uncertainty over finite or countable outcomes and supports randomized algorithms, reliability, and data-driven systems.

children.title: Probability Spaces and Events
children.description: Students model uncertainty with outcomes, events, and axioms rather than intuition alone.

children.title: Union bounds and inclusion-exclusion for events
Conditional Probability and Independence
children.description: Conditioning updates a model after new information. Independence states exactly when one event does not change another.

children.title: Random Variables, Expectation, and Concentration
children.description: Random variables convert outcomes into quantities that can be summarized and bounded.

children.title: Distributions, expectation, and linearity of expectation
Markov and Chebyshev bounds and Markov-chain preview

topics.title: Number Theory, Modular Arithmetic, and Cryptographic Foundations
topics.description: Elementary number theory turns arithmetic structure into algorithms for security, hashing, coding, and symbolic computation.

children.title: Divisibility, Primes, and the Euclidean Algorithm
children.description: Divisibility and greatest common divisors reveal the structure needed for modular computation.

children.title: Congruences and Modular Arithmetic
children.description: Congruences make arithmetic wrap around a modulus while preserving rigorous algebraic rules.

children.title: Linear congruences and Chinese remainder theorem
Cryptography, Hashing, and Coding Connections
children.description: Applications show how number-theoretic assumptions protect information and detect errors.

topics.title: Recurrence Relations, Generating Functions, and Asymptotic Growth
topics.description: Recurrences describe self-referential processes. Generating functions and asymptotic notation reveal their long-run behavior.

children.title: Building Recurrence Models
children.description: Students translate recursive algorithms and discrete processes into initial conditions and recurrence equations.

children.title: Solving Recurrences
children.description: Several complementary techniques turn recursive definitions into explicit or asymptotic solutions.

children.title: Asymptotic Growth and Algorithm Analysis
children.description: Growth rates compare resource use at scale while ignoring inessential constants.

children.title: Polynomial, logarithmic, exponential, and factorial growth
Master-theorem patterns and empirical sanity checks

topics.title: Graph Theory Foundations and Structural Properties
topics.description: Graph theory models pairwise relationships and provides a common language for networks, dependencies, circuits, and combinatorial structure.

children.title: Graph Models and Representations
children.description: Students choose graph types and data representations that preserve the relationships relevant to a problem.

children.title: Simple graphs, multigraphs, directed and weighted graphs
Adjacency lists, matrices, and incidence structures
Paths, Cycles, and Connectivity
children.description: Reachability and connectivity characterize how information, flow, or influence can move through a network.

children.title: Planarity, Coloring, and Graph Invariants
children.description: Structural invariants bound what a graph can represent and support scheduling, layout, and resource allocation.

children.title: Cliques, independent sets, and chromatic bounds

topics.title: Trees, Matchings, Network Algorithms, and Discrete Optimization
topics.description: This unit turns graph structure into algorithms for hierarchy, routing, assignment, and optimization.

children.title: Trees and Spanning Trees
children.description: Trees are minimally connected graphs and the natural structure for hierarchy, recursion, and network backbones.

children.title: Rooted trees, traversals, and binary trees
Traversal and Shortest-Path Algorithms
children.description: Systematic traversal discovers structure, while shortest-path methods optimize movement through weighted networks.

children.title: Topological ordering of directed acyclic graphs
Matching, Stable Assignment, and Discrete Optimization
children.description: Matching problems formalize compatible assignments and introduce proof-based algorithm design.

topics.title: Boolean Algebra, Digital Logic, and Computation Structures
topics.description: Boolean algebra connects logical reasoning to the design, simplification, and verification of digital systems.

children.title: Boolean Operations and Laws
children.description: Boolean algebra gives symbolic rules for manipulating two-valued functions.

children.title: Identity, complement, distributive, and De Morgan laws
Normal Forms and Combinational Circuits
children.description: Canonical forms translate directly between specifications and gate-level implementations.

children.title: Logic gates, multiplexers, decoders, and adders
Sequential Logic and Computation Structures
children.description: State and time turn combinational logic into machines that store information and execute protocols.

children.title: Hazards, timing assumptions, and hardware verification

topics.title: Finite Automata, Regular Languages, and Parsing Foundations
topics.description: Automata and formal languages make computation itself a mathematical object, linking software patterns to hardware state machines.

children.title: Deterministic and Nondeterministic Automata
children.description: Finite automata recognize patterns using bounded memory. Nondeterminism offers an equivalent but often simpler description.

children.title: DFAs, transition functions, and accepted languages
Regular Expressions and Limits of Regularity
children.description: Regular expressions and automata describe the same language class, while nonregularity results expose finite-memory limits.

children.title: Context-Free Grammars and Parsing Foundations
children.description: Grammars describe nested syntax that finite automata cannot capture, providing a bridge to compilers and protocol formats.

topics.title: Countability, Computability, and Decidability
topics.description: Countability and computability establish fundamental limits: some sets cannot be enumerated and some precisely stated problems cannot be solved by any algorithm.

children.title: Countability and Diagonalization
children.description: Students compare infinite sizes and learn how diagonal arguments prove that no enumeration can be complete.

children.title: Uncountability of real numbers and function sets
Turing Machines and Encodings
children.description: A simple universal machine model clarifies what counts as an effective procedure.

children.title: Encoding programs, inputs, and mathematical objects
Undecidability and Reductions
children.description: Reductions transfer impossibility from a known unsolvable problem to a new one.

children.title: Recognizability, co-recognizability, and limits of verification

topics.title: Algorithm Correctness, Complexity, Reductions, and Integrated Applications
topics.description: The closing unit integrates proof, structure, and computation to distinguish correct algorithms from efficient ones and to communicate what remains infeasible or unknown.

children.title: Correctness and Resource Models
children.description: Students connect preconditions, invariants, postconditions, and termination to explicit measures of time and space.

children.title: Reasonable machine models and input size
Complexity Classes and Reductions
children.description: Complexity theory groups problems by required resources and uses reductions to compare their difficulty.

children.title: Integrated Applications and Capstone
children.description: A final investigation asks students to model, prove, implement, test, and explain one discrete system for their degree context.

children.title: CS: algorithm, language, or security model
Mathematics: rigorous combinatorial or graph-theoretic investigation
Computer Engineering: logic, state-machine, coding, or network design
